prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental discovery of topological insulators, the quantum spin Hall effect and protected edge and surface states

statement.case_for: Topological insulators are the discovery with the broadest base of support in the opening round (seven of eight members ranked it, five in their top three, and my own second place), and the support is warranted on the science. Kane and Mele supplied the conceptual origin, a Z2 invariant that forces protected boundary states. Molenkamp's group then saw the quantum spin Hall edge channels in HgTe wells in 2007, and Hasan's group saw the three-dimensional surface states by ARPES. That is a full arc from idea to measurement that has been reproduced by many independent groups over fifteen to twenty years, with a stable interpretation, and it spread to photonics, cold atoms and mechanics. Having read the other ballots, I now prefer it to my own opening first choice. A prize on it recognises a new class of quantum matter, which is the kind of basic discovery a Nobel prize should reward, and the timing is ripe or overdue.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real and not solved by any three-name slate. Mele is arguably as defensible as Kane, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp followed, Fu, Kane and Moore also contributed to the 3D case, and the credited list omits several of them. The 2016 prize on topological phases (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz) may also make some members see this as a continuation. Practical consequences remain modest and Majorana-related hopes are unproven. If the committee will not accept Hasan's inclusion or the omission of Mele, the case weakens and B013 becomes a cleaner theory-plus-experiment story, although it is younger.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first as a simple, general and rigorous organising principle (a bulk invariant dictating boundary states) that spread across solids, photonics, cold atoms and mechanics, while acknowledging that dropping Mele or choosing between Molenkamp and Hasan is a real allocation problem.
responses.response: I agree on the breadth of reach and share the same slate (Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan). I would still put the allocation problem at the centre of our discussion. Dropping Mele and BHZ cannot be justified on merit alone and rests on the three-person cap. My view is that the citation should name the topological insulator concept and the two decisive observations, and that the committee should be explicit that Mele's claim is about equal to Kane's. I do not think the breadth in other fields should count as extra merit for the prize, since the prize is for the discovery.

responses.point: Olsson prefers Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, treating the theory plus the 2007 HgTe observation as the key discovery and not wanting a four-way split that includes Hasan's 3D ARPES work.
responses.response: I take the point that the quantum spin Hall effect is the cleanest case, and Mele belongs there. My reservation is that the 2D result is the first half of the story, and the 3D work is what turned it into a general class of materials that spans Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3. Without Hasan the prize would honour a prediction and one experiment in a narrow system. I would accept your slate over mine if the committee thinks that the theory pair belongs together, but I think that choice leaves the 3D discovery unrecognised, and I would want that cost stated openly.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first and topological insulators only as third-ranked (B004 with Xue), preferring the 2D/QAH arc and wanting to avoid a bundle of separate discoveries, while deferring to condensed-matter colleagues.
responses.response: Your worry that 2D QSH, 3D topological insulators and QAH are separate discoveries is fair, and it is one reason I would keep Xue's quantum anomalous Hall work out of this prize. I do not think that bundling the 2D and 3D observations under one concept is the same as bundling unrelated results, because they test one prediction (a nonzero bulk invariant fixes boundary states). On clocks, I see the physics as strong and mature but, as a non-specialist in precision metrology, I will defer to you and Kroll on whether the lattice clock is distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes. That is an argument about distinctness from earlier prizes that I cannot settle.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as the clearest case of experiment surprising theory, with quantitative band theory and many reproductions, and ranks topological insulators second while noting more than three strong claimants and the overlap with the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I agree that twisted bilayer graphene is a strong candidate and I ranked it third. My concern is maturity: the pairing mechanism is unsettled, twist-angle disorder complicates reproducibility, and it is about eight years since the 2018 experiments. On overlap with 2016, I would say the 2016 prize was about topological phase transitions and Hall conductance in model systems, and this one is about materials with protected boundary states, so I regard it as distinct but I accept the committee may want to say so in the citation. If you can show the correlated phases are robust across labs despite the disorder, I would move B013 up.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can justify omitting Mele (and the BHZ proposers) from a three-person slate, and whether Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a better trio than Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan.
How much weight the 2016 topological phases prize should carry against this discovery.

Whether circuit QED (B029) is premature or too close to the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, and whether twisted bilayer graphene is mature enough given the unsettled pairing mechanism.
statement.conflict_note: I rank circuit QED (B029) first in my opening ballot, and I am the director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a theorist in the Chalmers superconducting-circuits community, with Chalmers colleagues linked to the field and the dynamical Casimir work. That is a connection that may call for recusal or a discount of my views on B029 and I have therefore placed it only as an alternative. I also work in the area close to that candidate. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B024, B013 or the other shortlisted candidates.
